title: Why electrolytes have become wine’s newest additive
summary:
Joel Gott Wines has released Sauvy B, a canned Sauvignon Blanc spritz with electrolytes from pink Himalayan salt – the latest sign that 'functional' hydration ingredients are moving into wine.

The post Why electrolytes have become wine’s newest additive appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Joel Gott Wines has released Sauvy B, a canned Sauvignon Blanc spritz with electrolytes from pink Himalayan salt – the latest sign that 'functional' hydration ingredients, long confined to sports drinks and hangover cures, are moving into wine.

The 4.5% ABV product launched on 15 July in Lime and Grapefruit flavours, priced at US$13.99 for a four-pack, with initial distribution through Target, Walmart and Total Wine & More.

Each 12 fluid ounce (355ml) can blends sparkling water, citrus flavouring and a small proportion of California Sauvignon Blanc – roughly 9%, according to the brand – with the remainder made up of sparkling water, a formulation designed to keep the drink light, at around 100 calories per can, while still trading on the 'wine' name.

Sauvy B is a Joel Gott Wines release, but the company behind it is Trinchero Family Wine and Spirits,  the third-largest wine supplier in the US, whose portfolio also includes Three Thieves.

Founder Joel Gott, working with his wife and winemaking partner Sarah Gott, has described the launch as a recruitment tool for younger drinkers rather than a product for existing wine consumers, telling VinePair that getting the word "wine" into younger consumers' everyday vocabulary is central to building the next generation of wine drinkers.

Why electrolytes, why now

The addition of electrolytes taps a hydration-drinks boom that has, until now, run largely parallel to the wine and RTD alcohol categories rather than as part of them.

Fortune Business Insights puts the global electrolyte drinks market at roughly $43 billion in 2026, forecasting annual growth of around 8.4% through 2034, with ready-to-drink formats accounting for the dominant share. That growth has been driven by younger, “wellness-oriented” consumers already primed to look for hydration and "clean label" cues on brands.

Sauvy B is not the first alcoholic drink to draw from that world, but it is among the most prominent wine-based entrants.

Trinchero's move follows other low-ABV, electrolyte-branded launches this year, including Stateside Brands' vodka-based Super Lyte and Svedka's Vodka Water, both also formulated at 4.5% ABV — suggesting a standard is forming around that strength for "functional" RTDs.

A wine RTD problem the format is trying to solve

The launch also arrives at a pointed moment for wine-based RTDs specifically. Spirit-based ready-to-drinks have continued to take share from wine- and malt-based formats in recent years, and wine has struggled to establish the same foothold in canned formats that seltzers and spirit RTDs have secured with younger drinkers.

Sauvy B's pitch – a recognisable varietal name, a hydration angle and a price point pitched at mainstream grocery – is a direct attempt to close that gap rather than compete on wine credentials alone.

For the trade, the bigger story may be less about one brand than about ingredient positioning: electrolytes joining "low sugar," "gluten-free" and "low calorie" as a standard functional claim on wine-adjacent packaging.

Whether that proves durable – or fades the way flavoured hard seltzer's early wave did – will depend on whether retailers see repeat purchase once the novelty wears off. National rollout is scheduled to continue through January 2027, alongside planned pineapple and watermelon flavour extensions.

title: Bordeaux marks milestones with commemorative bottles
summary:
Bordeaux loves an anniversary, particularly when it coincides with an exceptional vintage. From the newly released 2025s to rare golden bottles from earlier decades, these commemorative editions combine fine wine with some of the region’s most collectable packaging.

The post Bordeaux marks milestones with commemorative bottles appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Bordeaux loves an anniversary, particularly when it coincides with an exceptional vintage. From the newly released 2025s to rare golden bottles from earlier decades, these commemorative editions combine fine wine with some of the region’s most collectable packaging. Bordeaux loves a milestone and, if it falls in an exceptional vintage, all the better. A couple of recently released 2025s celebrate significant anniversaries, and it is a wonderful vintage in which to do so. Exceptional weather conditions produced limited yields but stunning quality, even if the market did not respond enthusiastically across the board to the en primeur offer. Here are a few bottles that should be on your shopping list, both for the beauty of the wine and the bottles in which they come.

Château Gruaud Larose turns 300

Château Gruaud Larose, the second growth of Saint-Julien, celebrated its 300th anniversary in 2025 and has produced the bottle to prove it. Established in 1725 by Joseph-Stanislas Gruaud, it became known as Gruaud Larose in the 18th century. The château was built in 1879 by Baron Sarget, who gave his name to the estate’s second wine, Sarget de Gruaud Larose. Jean Merlaut and his family bought the property in 1997. The bottle for the 300th vintage is etched and screen-printed with golden leaves from the Cabernet Sauvignon vine, the signature grape variety of the Médoc. Appropriately, Cabernet Sauvignon represents 77% of the 2025 blend. It is available in bottle, magnum, double magnum, imperial and jeroboam formats. Buying en primeur means collectors can not only choose their preferred size but also customise larger formats for a special occasion of their own to commemorate.

A century of Brane-Cantenac

In Margaux, another second growth, Château Brane-Cantenac is celebrating its 100th anniversary under the ownership of the Lurton family with a special golden label for the 2025 vintage. Léonce Récapet acquired Brane-Cantenac in 1925 and the property has remained in the family for five generations. Léonce’s daughter Denise married François Lurton in 1923, and their second son, Lucien, inherited Brane-Cantenac in 1954. Living well into his 90s, Lucien became known as one of the great architects of the Médoc, bequeathing his love of wine and vineyards to his children. Henri Lurton has overseen the estate since 1992. In 2022, he passed ownership to his children while continuing to lead the management of the property. The embossed sun on the golden label was inspired by a raised medallion discovered on a 19th-century bottle of Brane-Cantenac. It is appropriate given that sunshine is a defining theme of the vintage, but also serves as a fitting tribute to Lucien Lurton, whose name means ‘bringer of light’.

Bordeaux’s golden years

There is a long tradition of golden bottles in Bordeaux. Château Mouton Rothschild released its 2000 vintage in a bottle decorated with a golden Augsburg Ram. Since 1945, the château has commissioned an artist to create a label for each vintage. For the millennium vintage, Baroness Philippine de Rothschild decided to make the bottle itself a work of art, as well as paying homage to the name of the property. The design was inspired by the Augsburg Ram, a 16th-century silver-gilt drinking vessel from the collection of the château’s Museum of Wine in Art. Relief-enamelled directly onto the glass, a golden ring around the neck of the bottle echoes the collar around the ram’s neck. The coat of arms, property name, vintage and signature are also screen-printed onto the bottle in gold. The 2000 vintage was exceptional and the arrival of the new millennium made it particularly auspicious. The market loved it. Released at a négociant price of €250, it is now trading at around €1,550.

Angélus celebrates promotion

In 2012, Château Angélus created a golden version of its characteristic bell label to celebrate its promotion to Premier Grand Cru Classé A. The technique used a similar raised enamelling process at 600°C, after which the bottle was covered with 21.7-carat gold and fired at 500°C. The year also marked the 230th anniversary of the Boüard de Laforest family’s arrival in Saint-Émilion. Some large formats remain on the market, ranging from magnums to 18-litre melchiors. Although the bottle does not command the same premium as the Mouton Rothschild 2000, it is trading at more than double its release price despite coming from a less celebrated vintage.

Château Margaux honours Paul Pontallier

In 2015, Château Margaux released a striking golden bottle to commemorate not only an exceptional vintage, there is something about Bordeaux years ending in five, but also an historic year for the estate. It marked the bicentenary of the château’s buildings, which date from 1815, and the inauguration of new facilities designed by architect Norman Foster. It was also the final vintage overseen by Paul Pontallier, managing director of Château Margaux from 1989 to 2015, and the bottle serves as a tribute to him. A magnificent screen print of the Palladian château was applied directly to the glass, replacing the classic label.

Talbot marks a century of family ownership

In 2018, Château Talbot, also in Saint-Julien, celebrated 100 years of ownership by the Cordier family, which remains at the helm of the estate today. The elegant silk-screened image on the bottle represents one of the pillars supporting the barrel cellar, which in turn evokes the vines rooted in the terroir. It is a modern and original design.

A celebratory year for Bordeaux

The excellent 2020 vintage prompted the release of several commemorative bottles. Château Léoville Poyferré, keeping Saint-Julien particularly busy, celebrated the centenary of the Cuvelier family’s ownership. Today, Sarah Lecompte Cuvelier represents the fourth generation of the family at the helm. The gold-inlaid bottle cleverly depicts the terroir of the property. Further north, the vintage marked both the 200th anniversary of Château Cos d’Estournel and 20 years of ownership by Michel Reybier. Its golden bottle was decorated with an image of the estate’s distinctive Asian-inspired architecture, which dominates the approach to Saint-Estèphe. Château Smith Haut Lafitte and Château Ducru-Beaucaillou also released celebratory bottles in 2020, although both opted for redesigned labels rather than fully decorated glass. As well as redesigning its label, Château Ducru-Beaucaillou etched its 300th anniversary in the estate’s signature orange on the shoulder of the bottle. Château Smith Haut Lafitte created a striking black and gold label for both its red and white wines to celebrate 30 years of ownership by the Cathiard family.

Collectable anniversary cases

There are also several recent anniversary collections worth seeking out, should you be able to find them. Château Rauzan-Gassies, the second growth of Margaux, is celebrating the 90th anniversary of its purchase by the Quié family. Paul Quié bought the vineyard in 1946 and, since 2000, the property has been run by his grandchildren, twins Anne-Françoise and Jean-Philippe. To celebrate this three-generation history, the estate created a wooden case containing six bottles, with two bottles from each of three important vintages. The 1966 vintage honours their grandfather Paul Quié, the 1996 commemorates his son Jean-Michel Quié and the 2016 celebrates the current owners, Anne-Françoise and Jean-Philippe Quié.

Between two Barton birthdays

There is another celebratory collection from the Barton family, owners of Châteaux Léoville Barton and Langoa Barton. The year 2021 marked the 200th anniversary of the Bartons’ arrival in Saint-Julien, when the family purchased Château Langoa Barton. To celebrate, the estate launched a label hand-drawn by Anne-Lise Yandell. A collection of four images traces the family’s history, focusing on origin, heritage, nature and evolution, all of which are signatures of the property and the family. Together, they form a distinctive and colourful label for the celebratory 2021 vintage of Château Langoa Barton. The individual images also appear in limited-edition packaging designed by Patrice Begnier, containing bottles of the 1994, 2000, 2009 and 2016 vintages alongside a magnum of 2021 that brings all four images together. Only 200 coffrets were produced. The year 2026 marks the 200th anniversary of Château Léoville Barton. The estate is looking to the past for its celebratory label, reviving the famous Art Deco design used by the property from the 1930s until the 1960s. Fingers are crossed for the vintage.

Looking to Bordeaux’s future

Not all celebratory collections look backwards. Château Grand-Puy-Lacoste, the classified growth of Pauillac, christened its new gravity-fed cellar with the 2025 vintage. The vintage represents the culmination of a decade-long renovation of the vineyards and cellar led by François-Xavier Borie and his daughter Emeline, who now heads the family estate. The 2025 bottle is screen-printed with an image of the elegant château. It is available in 75cl bottles, magnums, double magnums and imperials, including mixed cases containing different sizes for those unable to make up their minds.

Bottles worth keeping

These commemorative bottles are beautiful both inside and out, serving as elegant and long-lasting souvenirs of Bordeaux’s past and future. In some cases, they may also prove to be a good investment.

title: #WeekInPictures: the Queen visits Plumpton as craft beer and rum move into new territory
summary:
Her Majesty The Queen marked Plumpton College’s centenary during a visit to its Sussex campus, where she met students across wine, animal care and bakery programmes. Elsewhere, Vapoura Rum turned The Mandrake into music, American craft breweries gathered in Soho and judging began for the World Beer Awards 2026.

The post #WeekInPictures: the Queen visits Plumpton as craft beer and rum move into new territory appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Her Majesty The Queen marked Plumpton College’s centenary during a visit to its Sussex campus, where she met students across wine, animal care and bakery programmes. Elsewhere, Vapoura Rum turned The Mandrake into music, American craft breweries gathered in Soho and judging began for the World Beer Awards 2026.

The Queen marks Plumpton College centenary

Her Majesty The Queen visited Plumpton College on 7 July as part of its centenary celebrations. A patron of both the Plumpton College Charitable Foundation and WineGB, she toured the college’s 800-hectare estate and met students working across animal care, veterinary studies, wine and bakery. The visit included the college’s new lemur enclosure, canine hydrotherapy facilities and its Digital Centenary Vineyard. Her Majesty also explored the recently rebranded Plumpton Estate wine range before unveiling a plaque commemorating 100 years of land and environmental education at the South Downs campus.

Vapoura Rum turns The Mandrake into vinyl

Vapoura Rum launched The After Stories, a six-track vinyl EP inspired by the spaces of The Mandrake hotel in Fitzrovia. Producers CARALUS and Daniel Sehnawi translated rooms including Waeska, YOPO and the Masha Hari Theatre into music, with each track intended to capture the atmosphere of a particular corner of the hotel. A companion cocktail menu ran across The Mandrake’s bars, using Vapoura Chapter One and Chapter Two in serves including Angel Sage, Velvet Cocoon and Sacred Bean. One copy of the record was framed permanently at the hotel, with a limited number released to the public.

American craft beer meets Japanese cooking in Soho

The Brewers Association brought six US craft breweries to Moi in Soho for a dinner pairing beer with the restaurant’s Japanese-inspired menu. Sierra Nevada Summerfest Pilsner was served with Porthilly oysters, while Embolden Beer Co’s Midnight in Tokyo Matcha Hazy IPA met steamed fried buns with bluefin tuna. Deschutes Black Butte Porter accompanied wagyu nigiri, ColdFire’s wine barrel aged The Sparrow & The Crow was poured with dry-aged sirloin and The Virginia Beer Co’s Ideas of Order closed the meal beside raspberry whey sorbet.

World Beer Awards judging gets underway

db beer and features editor Jessica Mason joined brewers, writers and educators to judge entries for the World Beer Awards 2026. Beers from around the world were assessed across roughly 40 styles ahead of the final stage next month. Mason judged alongside Adrian Tierney Jones, Bill Simmons and Pete Brown.

title: Spirits industry responds to US lifting tariffs on Scotch
summary:
The US has officially returned to tariff-free trading for Scotch whisky in a move that has been met by much goodwill among the sector.

The post Spirits industry responds to US lifting tariffs on Scotch appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
The US has officially returned to tariff-free trading for Scotch whisky in a move that has been met by much goodwill among the sector. US President Donald Trump had originally imposed a 10% levy on Scotch whisky in April 2025 which had been due to increase earlier this year to 25% for single malts. However, the decision to make sure Scotch whisky would be exempt from tariffs, which came into force as of today (24 July) was made by Trump following King Charles III’s state visit in April this year. The Scottish government and the spirits industry has welcomed the lifting of tariffs on Scotch whisky exports to the US, which could also see Bourbon and American whiskey arriving in the UK tariff-free. The tariff removal follows a challenging period for Scotch whisky exports. According to the Scotch Whisky Association (SWA), shipments to the US fell sharply after a 10% tariff was introduced in April 2025. In fact, the SWA had noted that export volumes declined by 15% between May and December 2025, with the US still staying as the industry’s most valuable overseas market despite the downturn.

Win-win

Scotland's first minister John Swinney said: “The result is a ‘zero-for-zero’ tariff regime that is a win for Scotland and a win for the United States. It benefits businesses and workers on both sides of the Atlantic and not just among whisky producers but also the businesses and communities that support the sector across Scotland. This is a good day for Scotland.” Distilled Spirits Council president and CEO Chris Swonger said: “We thank President Trump for delivering on his commitment to remove the tariff on Scotch and other UK whiskies and for recognising the longstanding heritage, craftsmanship and distilling traditions that unite the United States and United Kingdom.”

'Much-needed relief'

Swonger pointed out that “lifting this tariff provides much-needed relief for US hospitality businesses and demonstrates the benefits of fair, reciprocal trade” and added that “it is a meaningful step toward restoring the zero-for-zero tariff framework that fuelled growth, investment and job creation throughout the spirits sector for decades”. Highlighting the positive impact this will have on the Scotch whisky industry, through improved access to American consumers while supporting businesses at home, Nodjame Fouad, CEO of Pernod Ricard’s aged spirits and Champagne division, said: "The return to tariff-free trade for Scotch whisky between the UK and US - the world's most valuable Scotch whisky market - is very welcome news for our industry.

A long-standing trading relationship

Fouad explained: "This move will improve access for American consumers to iconic Scotch whiskies such as The Glenlivet, while supporting businesses at home, and strengthening the long-standing trading relationship between the UK and US spirits industries.” Swonger said that the Distilled Spirits Council now looks forward to working with the administration “to build on this progress by extending tariff relief to other imported spirits, particularly those from the European Union, which would help reduce costs for restaurants, bars and other hospitality businesses across the country”. Fouad also added: "We now hope to see further progress made towards the removal of tariffs affecting other spirits and wine categories - including Irish Whiskey, Champagne and Cognac - to deliver benefits for consumers, producers and hospitality businesses on both sides of the Atlantic."

title: Château d’Esclans eyes earliest harvest ever as it trials new grapes
summary:
Château d'Esclans, the Provence estate behind category-leading rosé Whispering Angel, is on course for the earliest harvest in its history – and is trialling grapes from Greece, Spain and Italy as part of a longer-term response to rising temperatures.

The post Château d’Esclans eyes earliest harvest ever as it trials new grapes appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Château d'Esclans, the Provence estate behind category-leading rosé Whispering Angel, is on course for the earliest harvest in its history – and is trialling grapes from Greece, Spain and Italy as part of a longer-term response to rising temperatures.

Speaking to db on 2 July, winemaker Joéva Walczak said the property expects to begin picking around 10 August, weeks ahead of its usual start. "We have very, very hot temperatures right now, and the vines are ok, but we are thinking about irrigation," she said. "We check the vines every day, but we are fingers-crossed for a beautiful vintage – we don't have any disease, and we don't have any weather problems, except for maybe the high temperatures, and we think we will begin the harvest around 10 August, which is very, very early." Asked whether this would be the earliest harvest on record for the estate, she confirmed it would be: "Even in 2018 and 2020 it wasn't that early – and our cellar master Jean-Claude Neu said that ten years ago, we would harvest as school started, which was the beginning of September."

Adapting in the vineyard

Château d'Esclans makes a range of wines, from barrel-fermented fine rosés such as Garrus and Les Clans through to Whispering Angel, sourced from grapes across Côtes de Provence. Walczak said the estate is making a number of changes in both vineyard and cellar to cope with the heat. In the vineyard, keeping the soils covered with grasses is one technique for keeping ground-level temperatures down and, perhaps counterintuitively, for retaining soil moisture. As db has reported on previously, a permanent ground cover improves soil structure and provides a mulch through the hot months, lowering soil temperature and boosting organic matter so that the soil absorbs and retains more water when it does rain. Irrigation is permitted in Provence, but with strict limits on timing and quantity, while vineyard yields are capped. In the cellar, keeping the wines cool and protected is a priority: inert gas is used to guard against oxidation, and equipment keeps grapes, musts and wines cool throughout. The estate also uses the white grape Rolle — known as Vermentino across the Italian border — co-fermented with the region's red grapes, chief among them Grenache, to bring freshness to the wines.

New grapes on trial

Provence's pink wines are built primarily around Grenache, alongside Cinsault, Mourvèdre, Syrah, some Tibouren and Rolle. Since December 2021, however, new varieties have been permitted on an experimental basis for AOP Provence rosés. These include Rousseli — an ancient, near-extinct local white/pink variety also known as Rosé du Var — the Greek varieties Agiorgitiko, Moschofilero and Xinomavro, Italy's Calabrese (also widely known as Nero d'Avola), and Spain's drought-resistant white grape Verdejo, most famous for Rueda's crisp whites. Château d'Esclans has planted two of the new reds — Nero d'Avola and Xinomavro — and one white, Verdejo. Walczak stressed it remains "just an experiment for now," but said that if the varieties deliver the quality and freshness the estate is looking for, they could eventually feature in its rosé blends, including Whispering Angel. Grenache will remain the backbone of the wines regardless, she said, describing it as "the star" of Provence rosé for its pale colour — a result of the grape's moderate levels of anthocyanins (natural plant pigments) — and fruity character. It also performs well when fermented and aged in oak, even as a rosé: Walczak pointed to the "successful marriage" of wood and Grenache-based pink wines. The barrel-driven approach to Château d'Esclans' top rosés, she said, was "inspired by white Burgundy, but now we have our own approach: the Château d'Esclans process."
