title: Andreola: the quiet exit from Prosecco
summary:
Forty years after Nazzareno Andreola founded the estate that bears his name, his son has spent much of his tenure doing something that looks, on paper, like commercial self-sabotage: taking the word Prosecco off the label. James Bayley met him to talk about steep hillsides, vanishing labour and the risk of giving up the most valuable word in Italian wine.

The post Andreola: the quiet exit from Prosecco appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Forty years after Nazzareno Pola founded the estate, his son has spent much of his tenure doing something that looks, on paper, like commercial self-sabotage: taking the word Prosecco off the label. James Bayley met him to talk about steep hillsides, vanishing labour and the risk of giving up the most valuable word in Italian wine. The conversation follows on from db's recent visit to Andreola's newer project in the Belluno Dolomites, Andreola takes Prosecco expertise into the Dolomites, where Stefano Pola is applying the same instinct for territory over category to a nine-hectare vineyard well outside Valdobbiadene DOCG. The times, the knowledge and the technologies of 1984 bear little relation to those of today, but the path Nazzareno Pola set out has held. "Forty years later we are still here talking about quality," his son, Stefano, tells db. Since then the estate has been built into a benchmark within Valdobbiadene DOCG, expanding on several fronts at once even as fresh challenges keep appearing. New projects and new areas of business are already under way. That growth has been rapid, moving from a small family winery selling locally to a medium-sized company with a far larger vineyard holding, a more complex winery operation and a commercial structure that now reaches export markets. Stefano counts the management of that transition among his proudest achievements, not for its scale but for what it did not cost. "I have worked to provide the right support across all production departments, creating the conditions for quality not only to be preserved, but to improve continuously as the company evolved."

Two hundred and fifty parcels, one principle

The estate now farms around 250 parcels across roughly 110 hectares, a spread that could easily have diluted the identity of any single vineyard. He bought into the Rive of Valdobbiadene DOCG at a point when other producers were doing the opposite, trading steep and difficult sites for large, flat vineyards that were easier and cheaper to farm. "Even if it means going against the current, quality comes first."

Heroism, minus the marketing

The phrase 'heroic viticulture' has drifted into most producers' vocabulary by now, deployed wherever a hillside needs dressing up for an export market. Andreola is careful to separate the term from what it actually costs on his own slopes. Climate change sits underneath everything, but the harder problem, he says, is finding people willing to do the work at all. Vineyard labour follows nature's timetable rather than anyone's rota, and that rhythm sits badly with a younger workforce. Summer starts before dawn to dodge the heat and often resumes in the evening once it has passed, a pattern that no longer suits every employee's expectations. Wet springs compound it: three or four days locked out of the vineyard by rain, followed by a single dry weekend that cannot wait for Monday. "Nature sets the timetable, and everyone involved should be willing to step in and carry out the most urgent tasks whenever the opportunity arises." What makes the territory difficult is also what makes it distinctive. Varied soils, altitudes and exposures, worked through the versatility of Glera, give Andreola a spread of styles running from Extra Brut to Dry, each one tied unmistakably to where it was grown.

The human factor

Ask Stefano who matters most in all this and the answer arrives without hesitation: the growers and vineyard workers who farm the steepest ground. "Without them, we would not have the opportunity to benefit from the excellent raw material we need in order to transform it into our wines." What strikes him about a historic wine village is how thoroughly the whole community absorbs the rhythm of the vineyard year, whether they work in it directly or not. "From the pharmacist to the mechanic, everyone has a general understanding of how to grow a vine or, in some way, how to prune it." Come September, the village itself seems to pause for harvest. It is, he says, the most beautiful element of terroir: not the soil, but the people standing on it. He is banking on that knowledge passing naturally from one generation to the next, carried more by proximity than by any formal scheme.

Dropping the name that made them famous

No decision at Andreola has drawn more scrutiny than the removal of the word Prosecco from its labels, a process Stefano began weighing in 2007 and completed by 2018. His own explanation starts with a question: Prosecco made the estate famous, but famous for what, exactly? "Every winery has to find its own interpretation," he says, and Andreola's has been to let the name of the territory do the talking instead, tying the wine unmistakably to a place already recognised for quality. Before the current appellation system arrived in 2009, the job abroad was simple: introduce people to the product and explain what it was. Now the job is subtler and harder, spent explaining the gap between a flatland Prosecco and a hillside Valdobbiadene DOCG, between a wine built for volume and one built for quality. Not everyone in the region has made peace with that gap, many of the older producers remain firmly opposed, having built the name Prosecco's fame themselves in the Conegliano Valdobbiadene area in the first place. Giving it up reads to some as a moral defeat, handing the keys of a Ferrari to producers who arrived later and now share in a reputation they did not build. Andreola's own decision, once made, came without much hand wringing. The estate no longer wanted to be tied to a Prosecco category that had grown too broad and too simplified for what it was trying to say, quite apart from the reputation the word had picked up along the way. It was not an easy call, but the results are already visible: customers now read Andreola as a producer standing apart, rooted in the historic area, practising heroic viticulture and priced accordingly on the strength of it. "We believe we made the right decision in pursuing it." He has some sympathy for wineries too frightened to make the same move, but not much patience for avoiding the question. If thirty years of marketing has hung on the word Prosecco in large type and an affordable price, then dropping it is a real risk. But if the story has always been about territory and a handcrafted, high-quality product, the word may simply no longer be doing much work. "Then perhaps that message has already become strong enough, and the word Prosecco may no longer be necessary," Stefano concludes.

Tasting notes by Patrick Schmitt MW:

1 – 26°I° Valdobbiadene DOCG Rive di Col San Martino Extra Brut Orchard fruit aromatics, dominated by fresh pear, and a floral note of star jasmine. The palate is zesty, fresh, with creamy bubbles and a lemony finish. Ripe pear and apple fruit feature first, while the finish is quite firm – this is a pure, clean and fruity but very dry style of Prosecco. 2 – DIRUPO Valdobbiadene DOCG Brut Creamy and appealing nose with a touch of pineapple and peach, ripe and sweet smelling. The palate is rounded and full, with sweet peach and some pineapple chunk. Fine bubbles provide a cleansing sensation, augmented by some fresh, balancing acidity on the finish. An easy drinking, refreshing, slightly sweet style of first-rate Prosecco, with some bitter pith on the finish, and lots of flavour persistence. 3 – Mas de Fer Rive di Soligo Valdobbiadene DOCG Extra Dry Enticing aromas of ripe orchard fruits. The palate is rich in creamy-textured bubbles, ripe apple and pear fruit, then lovely juicy peach, and a pleasant mouth-filling sweetness. The finish is fresh, with some crisp apple and lemon zest. Lingering, with some fine phenolic grip, then a subtle bitter lemon edge. Sweetest of the three, but still refreshing.

title: Lucky Saint and Ossett Brewery join Cask Marque
summary:
Beer quality accreditation organisation Cask Marque has welcomed Lucky Saint and Ossett Brewery as corporate members. Jessica Mason reports.

The post Lucky Saint and Ossett Brewery join Cask Marque appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Beer quality accreditation organisation Cask Marque has welcomed Lucky Saint and Ossett Brewery as corporate members. Jessica Mason reports. The companies join the stakeholders in the not-for-profit scheme which currently has 41 members made up of brewers, pub retailers and trade associations. Ossett Brewery currently has all of its own pubs accredited with Cask Marque already. But, by joining as a corporate member, the new move will allow Ossett to share benefits with its free trade outlets while also receiving beer quality reports on products assessed by Cask Marque anywhere in the UK. Lucky Saint joins as Cask Marque expands accreditations to include all beer with the new Perfect Pint Promise accreditation. With the rapid growth of the low and no alcohol category, the UK’s biggest independent alcohol-free beer brand continues to ensure standards are high through its own quality programme.

Improving beer quality and yields

Describing the reasons behind becoming a corporate member, Ossett Brewery managing director Edd Simpson said: ”We have worked with Cask Marque in our own pub estate and seen the benefits. We now want to take this support to our free trade customers so they can improve yields and with improved beer quality, their rate of sale and ensure our products are served in the best possible condition.” Speaking to the drinks business, Cask Marque executive director Paul Nunny admitted that he recognised the "potential" within the burgeoning low and no beer sector and said: “Draught in low and no is effectively a new sector with great potential growth.” Making assurances about beer quality checks, Nunny told db that Cask Marque has “set standards on production through Salsa + Beer that check beer quality at the brewery gate” and also added that the accreditation organisation has “worked with BBPA and gained their input and approval”. Nunny explained that “in pubs, beer lines must be cleaned every seven days as beer with no alcohol can quickly become contaminated and can increase in alcohol strength” and revealed that, because of this the organisation is already “working closely with Diageo and Heineken and now Lucky Saint”.

A shrewd move as the category continues to grow

Highlighting the fact that "quality has always been fundamental to Lucky Saint and speaking more broadly on how delivering on that quality ad supporting pubs and people with the best experiences possible was fundamental,  Lucky Saint on-trade director Will Snowden said: "From brewing to dispense, every stage plays a role in delivering a great alcohol-free beer experience. As more venues expand their alcohol-free draught offer, maintaining consistently high standards is vital. It’s an area we think deserves a lot of time and attention, and I'm very pleased to be working closer with Cask Marque as their first-ever alcohol-free beer member. Alongside our own Superior Serve programme, the Perfect Pint Promise accreditation will help support pubs in delivering the highest quality alcohol-free beer as this category continues to grow.” Looking at the business angle too, Nunny additionally pointed out that, for a pub, “having a product on draught can increase throughputs by seven times” but, he warned that it was only suitable for some pubs with the throughput because the publican “must sell a keg a week to maintain beer quality”.

Customers' expectations have never been higher

He also pointed out how important the accreditation was and insisted that “customers’ expectations on their visit to the pub have never been higher and these need to be satisfied” and highlighted that “this can be achieved by serving great beer and having trained bar staff". Offering reassurances, Nunny said: "This is why we now star rate cellar like the food hygiene ratings and have widened our accreditations to include Cask Marque and well as the new Perfect Pint Promise accreditation covering all beer". This, he reiterated, was why it was so important to have the support of beer businesses that are also interested in maintaining the calibre of beer brands they make available to pubs and bars. Not just when the beer leaves the brewery, but at each venue, in each cellar and at each point of sale. He added: "Having corporate members support is so important to deliver our programme on the perfect serve. The input from our new members will assist us to achieve this objective.”

title: Reasons to visit ProWine Mumbai
summary:
ProWine is set to take place on November 18–19, 2026, at the Jio World Convention Centre, Mumbai. db finds out more about what to expect.

The post Reasons to visit ProWine Mumbai appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
ProWine is set to take place on November 18–19, 2026, at the Jio World Convention Centre, Mumbai. db finds out more about what to expect. ProWine Mumbai brings together an unmatched mix of Indian and international wine and spirits producers, importers, distributors, country pavilions, trade promotion bodies, and allied beverage businesses. Jointly organised by Messe Düsseldorf India and All Things Nice, ProWine Mumbai is set to strengthen its position as the definitive business platform connecting global producers with India’s rapidly evolving beverage market. Bringing together industry leaders, importers, distributors, HORECA professionals, and premium consumers, the 2025 edition hosted more than 200 exhibitors, welcomed over 6,000 attendees, and saw participation from more than 20 countries, showcasing over 1,000 labels from across the globe.

Strong international representation

This year, while the final exhibitor roster continues to evolve, attendees can expect participation from leading global wine regions alongside premium Indian producers, craft beverage companies, spirits brands, and suppliers across packaging, technology, logistics, glassware, and accessories. The event has historically featured strong international representation through country pavilions from markets including France, Italy, Australia, Japan, Ireland, Germany, the UK, the US and others.

A place to gain insight

Speaking to the drinks business about what makes the show a must-visit event, ProWine Mumbai project director Rajeev Naresh said: “For wine and spirits professionals, ProWine Mumbai is more than a trade exhibition—it's a business platform. It offers opportunities to discover new products, meet producers and importers face-to-face, identify distribution partners, understand emerging consumer trends, attend expert-led masterclasses, and gain insights into India's rapidly evolving beverage market.” Naresh explained that “the combination of high-quality networking and curated educational content makes it an essential event for anyone looking to grow their business in the sector”. Mumbai is India's commercial and financial capital and the country's most influential market for premium wines and spirits. It is home to many of India's leading importers, distributors, hospitality groups, retailers, and beverage decision-makers, making it the ideal location for meaningful business conversations.  

Conveniently located

Giving more explanation about the event’s location, Naresh told db that “its proximity to Nashik, India's largest wine-producing region, excellent international connectivity, access to the country's busiest beverage import gateway, and world-class exhibition infrastructure further strengthen its position as the natural home for ProWine Mumbai”. Additionally, Naresh explained that “what differentiates ProWine Mumbai is its ability to combine business with education and innovation. Beyond the exhibition floor, visitors can experience curated masterclasses, tastings at the booths, panel discussions, bartender competitions and the newly introduced ProWine Zero segment, reflecting growing consumer interest in premium spirits and low- and no-alcohol beverages. These features ensure attendees leave with both valuable commercial connections and a deeper understanding of emerging market trends”. Looking at what is achievable, he pointed out that “the overarching goal of ProWine Mumbai is to strengthen its position as India's definitive international business platform for the wine and spirits industry while facilitating meaningful trade opportunities between domestic and global stakeholders”.

Unmissable business potential for the drinks sector

Indeed, Naresh also noted that “success is measured not only by growth in exhibitor and visitor numbers, but also by the quality of business generated, international participation, buyer engagement, educational programming, and the long-term partnerships formed through the event.” He insisted: “One of the strongest indicators of the show's impact is the growing number of success stories that have emerged from previous editions. Several international wine and spirits producers that first showcased their portfolios at ProWine Mumbai have since secured import and distribution partnerships and successfully entered the Indian market.”  

A launchpad for brands to crack the Indian market

Naresh described how “these outcomes demonstrate the event's role as more than just a trade fair—it is a launchpad for brands seeking to establish a presence in one of the world's most dynamic and promising beverage markets.” Considering its format, Naresh reiterated that the success of each show “is also evaluated through metrics such as the number of participating countries, country pavilions, trade professionals attending, business meetings facilitated, and the expansion of emerging beverage categories represented on the show floor” Naresh reinforced that the event was not just important, but provided a “gateway” for drinks business owners to successfully establish themselves in India and added that “combined with the increasing number of brands using the platform to successfully enter India, the continued growth in exhibitor participation and international representation reinforces ProWine Mumbai's position as the preferred gateway for global wine and spirits companies looking to build long-term business in the Indian market”.

title: Why Mayfair’s BiBi Lates is worth staying out for
summary:
London restaurant BiBi has introduced a new late-night format, BiBi Lates, giving guests the chance to experience signature dishes alongside an expanded cocktail offering after dinner service.

The post Why Mayfair’s BiBi Lates is worth staying out for appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
London restaurant BiBi has introduced a new late-night format, BiBi Lates, giving guests the chance to experience signature dishes alongside an expanded cocktail offering after dinner service.

Award-winning London restaurant BiBi has launched BiBi Lates, a new evening concept designed to extend service beyond its regular dinner offering.

Available from 9pm onwards, the new format pairs an extended cocktail list with an à la carte menu featuring a selection of dishes from the restaurant's tasting menu.

Signature dishes served after dark

Guests visiting BiBi Lates can order dishes including Mangalori Scallops and Launceston Lamb Barra Kebab, offering a more flexible way to experience chef Chet Sharma's cooking without committing to the full tasting menu.

The restaurant said the new format is designed to allow diners to enjoy BiBi's atmosphere later into the evening while sampling a curated selection of its signature dishes.

BiBi takes its name from the South Asian word that formally means "lady of the house", although Sharma has adopted its colloquial Urdu meaning of "grandma" as a tribute to his two grandmothers, whose influence is woven throughout the restaurant.

Research-led approach

Opened in September 2021, BiBi's menus are underpinned by years of research into ingredients, with an emphasis on traceability and ethics. The restaurant sources dayboat-landed fish from British waters, hand-dived scallops from Devon, buffalo milk from Lancashire and cheese from Somerset, while using heritage rice varieties and single-source spices from the Indian subcontinent.

The kitchen also follows sustainability and zero-waste practices, including composting, recycling, fermentation, preservation and maximising the use of individual ingredients.

Alongside its food offering, BiBi serves a wine list designed to complement the menus, as well as reinvented classic cocktails, non-alcoholic juices and cold-brewed teas. The sommelier team, led by Wilem Powell, offers two wine pairings inspired by Sharma's grandfathers.

Since opening, the Mayfair restaurant has received a number of industry accolades, including Best Cocktail List of the Year at the National Restaurant Awards 2025.

title: Vintae completes Bodegas Riojanas acquisition
summary:
Vintae has completed its acquisition of Bodegas Riojanas after the registration of the winery's restructuring plan, giving the Rioja-based wine group a 90% stake in the historic producer.

The post Vintae completes Bodegas Riojanas acquisition appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Vintae has completed its acquisition of Bodegas Riojanas after the registration of the winery's restructuring plan, giving the Rioja-based wine group a 90% stake in the historic producer.

Vintae has completed its acquisition of Bodegas Riojanas after the registration of the winery's Restructuring Plan with the Commercial Registry, formalising the entry of its holding company, Gevisa Wine Capital, as the majority shareholder.

The registration follows approval by Commercial Court No. 6 of Logroño and completes a process that began in May. Bodegas Riojanas will retain its status as a publicly listed company, with its shares continuing to trade on the Spanish continuous market.

Under the Restructuring Plan, Gevisa Wine Capital has acquired a 90% stake in Bodegas Riojanas through a capital reduction followed by a simultaneous capital increase via the capitalisation of debt.

The transaction represents a €12 million investment by Gevisa Wine Capital, following an agreement with the financial institutions that adhered to the Restructuring Plan. Vintae will also provide Bodegas Riojanas with a financing facility of up to €5 million to support the next phase of the business.

Board changes

The registration of the Restructuring Plan also brings changes to the board of Bodegas Riojanas.

Ricardo Arambarri Pérez has been appointed chairman, while Fernando Martínez Sampedro becomes chief executive officer. Isabel García Castellanos and Raúl Acha Salazar have joined the board as proprietary directors.

The company said two independent directors will be appointed in September in line with regulations governing publicly listed companies.

The deal has now entered its final administrative phase, which involves the admission to trading of the newly issued shares before the Spanish National Securities Market Commission (CNMV). According to the company, this process will not affect either the effectiveness of the transaction or the day-to-day operations of Bodegas Riojanas.

Expanding Vintae's portfolio

The acquisition adds several wineries and assets to the Vintae portfolio, including Bodegas Riojanas in Rioja, Bodegas Torreduero in Toro, Bodegas Viore in Rueda and a 56% stake in Veiga Naúm in Rías Baixas, together with their production assets, vineyards, facilities and commercial brands.

Founded in 1890, Bodegas Riojanas owns brands including Monte Real and Viña Albina. Vintae said the transaction marks the beginning of a new chapter for the winery, supported by a strengthened financial structure and the backing of a group with a commercial presence in Spain and more than 70 countries worldwide.

The company added that it will define Bodegas Riojanas' medium- and long-term development plan while reviewing the positioning of the group's companies and brands and gradually integrating processes, systems and management models.

Richi Arambarri, CEO of Vintae, said: "This transaction represents another important step in Vintae's evolution. Over the past few years, we have built a company with projects that are deeply rooted in their territories, supported by a solid business structure and strong commercial capabilities. That journey is what now enables us to take on a project of this scale with confidence and responsibility."

He added: "We begin this new chapter with the utmost respect for the identity of Bodegas Riojanas and with the conviction that we can help drive its future while preserving the value of its history and its brands."

title: Spain’s Juvé & Camps begins earliest-ever harvest
summary:
Spain's sparkling wine producer Juvé & Camps started its 2026 harvest at the Espiells estate today – the earliest start in the Sant Sadurní d'Anoia winery's history, and the first time the producer has picked at night.

The post Spain’s Juvé & Camps begins earliest-ever harvest appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Juvé & Camps started its 2026 harvest at the Espiells estate today – the earliest start in the Sant Sadurní d'Anoia winery's history, and the first time the producer has picked at night.

The centenarian house, which specialises in brut nature sparkling wines, has never before begun harvesting in July. High temperatures in recent weeks accelerated ripening on its earliest plots, pulling forward the optimum picking date and prompting the switch to night-time harvesting to avoid the worst of the daytime heat – with current highs hitting around 30 degrees Celsius.

Around 100 pickers are working alongside the winery's viticulture team over the coming weeks, harvesting entirely by hand and bunch by bunch, which allows an initial selection in the vineyard itself.

Night picking keeps the fruit cooler in transit, reducing oxidation risk and preserving aromatics, freshness and acidity, while also easing conditions for harvest workers.

Picking began with Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, destined for base wines for long-aged sparkling wines, with Macabeo, Xarel-lo and Parellada to follow as ripening progresses. Each plot is picked separately according to variety, orientation, altitude, soil and ripeness, with minimal time between picking and pressing given the vineyards' proximity to the winery.

Early harvest of healthy grapes

Despite the early start, the winery has described the season as favourable. Rainfall of 630mm since winter has replenished soil water reserves after several dry years, and pre-harvest checks show healthy, uniform fruit with gradual ripening and a good level of natural acidity.

Juvé & Camps is targeting around 1 million kg of grapes from its own vineyards, at an estimated average yield of 5,500 kg/ha, though final figures depend on weather over the coming weeks.

This compares to Champagne, where the 'marketable yield' has been capped at 8,800kg, the lowest this century, aside from 2020’s Covid-induced anomaly – when the region capped production at 8,000kg/ha.

"Winter rains have restored balance to the soils and allowed the vines to reach ripeness with much greater water availability than in recent years," said Pep Jiménez, viticulture director at Juvé & Camps.

"The grapes are healthy and uniform; now the challenge is to read each plot and harvest it at precisely the right moment, without letting the season's overall earliness dictate our decisions," he added.

Laura Tragant, technical director at the sparkling wine producer said that early samples pointed to "a highly promising combination of freshness, ripeness and natural acidity," adding: "Everything points to a balanced and distinctive vintage, with the ideal conditions to produce brut nature sparkling wines of remarkable depth."

First vintage since joining Corpinnat

This is Juvé & Camps' first harvest since joining Corpinnat, the collective brand whose production requirements include organically grown and vinified grapes, manual harvesting, estate vinification, extended ageing, external audits and a guaranteed minimum price for growers. For 2026, Juvé & Camps is guaranteeing partner growers a minimum €0.96/kg – a good price for the region, but significantly lower than Champagne, where as much as €7 per kg is paid.

The winery farms 252 hectares of estate vineyards across Espiells, La Cuscona and the higher-altitude Mediona sites — certified organic since 2015 and managed under regenerative principles, including cover crops, organic matter incorporation, gentle and green pruning, and plot-specific water management.

A detailed soils study at Espiells, based on 76 test pits and 260 soil borings, underpins its plot-by-plot approach. As part of its climate-adaptation work, the winery has also planted a new Xarel·lo vermell plot using the 'keyline design system', which follows land contours to improve water infiltration and reduce erosion.

Precision farming for value creation

"This harvest reflects a way of working that begins long before the grapes are picked: caring for the soil, tending each plot with precision, and always thinking for the long term," said Meritxell Juvé, CEO and fourth-generation family member.

"We want every vintage to remain true to the Penedès and for the value it creates to flow back to the people who keep this landscape alive."

Juvé & Camps is one of a number of European wine producers setting new records for harvest start dates, including Domaine Lafage in Roussillon, while estates in Provence and growers in Champagne are expecting to begin picking earlier than ever before in 2026.

title: English investor buys historic Château Vignelaure
summary:
English insurance entrepreneur Neil Utley has acquired Château Vignelaure, one of Provence’s most historically important wine estates. The deal brings new investment to a property renowned for pioneering Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah blends, but whose future direction remains open as rosé continues to dominate the region.

The post English investor buys historic Château Vignelaure appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
English insurance entrepreneur Neil Utley has acquired Château Vignelaure, one of Provence’s most historically important wine estates. The deal brings new investment to a property renowned for pioneering Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah blends, but whose future direction remains open as rosé continues to dominate the region. Following in the footsteps of countless celebrities and outside investors, English insurance tycoon Neil Utley bought Château Vignelaure on 23 July 2026. It is hard to overstate Vignelaure’s fame and importance to the late 20th-century Provence wine scene. The label for its second wine, Le Page, was designed by Yves Saint Laurent, and the estate’s connection to the arts has remained strong ever since.

A pioneer of Provence reds

Founded by Georges Brunet in 1960 in the northern part of Provence’s Coteaux d’Aix AOP, Vignelaure lies at more than 400 metres above sea level on the southern banks of the Durance river. The estate pioneered blends of Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah for red wines. Eloi Durrbach, who was working at Vignelaure at the time, was inspired by the approach and subsequently planted the same varieties at Trévallon.

A chequered ownership history

Since then, Vignelaure has had a chequered history, with most owners retaining the estate for only a few years. Among them was Maharajah Shivdasani, who also owned the historic Château Saint-Jean de Villecroze and the cru classé Château Galoupet, now owned by Moët Hennessy. He was followed by Irishman David O’Brien and, most recently, the art-collecting Danish-Swedish couple Mette and Bengt Sundstrøm, who acquired the property in 2007. The Sundstrøms appointed the current director and winemaker, Philippe Bru, in 2008. Utley has made clear that Bru will remain in charge of the estate.

Fine reds face a changing market

Once a hugely prestigious estate, and an inspiration for producers across the region alongside Trévallon, Vignelaure’s focus on muscular, age-worthy reds has left it at a difficult crossroads in a region where rosé is the driving force. The reds still follow the original Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah recipe, but Maison Saint Aix, one of Vignelaure’s closest neighbours about five kilometres to the north, produces rosé exclusively. Today, 40% of Vignelaure’s production is rosé, made in a very classical style, and 20% is white. The latter includes a substantial proportion of Sauvignon Blanc, which thrives in the northern Coteaux d’Aix, along the Durance valley and the Trévaresse hills. Only 40% of the estate’s 56 hectares of vines is now dedicated to its iconic reds.

Investment planned in vineyard and cellar

Significant investment is planned in both replanting the vineyard and updating the cellar, much of which dates from the winery’s last major renovation in 1972. As this is Utley’s first venture into the wine industry, it remains to be seen whether fine wine will become the estate’s central priority or whether, as with several former owners, Vignelaure will serve primarily as a base for Provençal living and an art collection. Plans have already been announced for a line of nature-inspired cosmetics called Maison Minu, made using grapeseed oil, olive oil and honey from the Vignelaure estate, alongside the construction of a spa.

Evolution rather than revolution

Bru is keen to avoid promises of sweeping changes to the wines. “Our plan is to keep going in the same style across all three colours, while improving quality, image and sales,” he said.

title: Why Billecart-Salmon waited 208 years to make a Ratafia
summary:
As Maison Billecart-Salmon gears up to launch its inaugural Ratafia Champenois in Asia this autumn, seventh generation owner Mathieu Roland-Billecart explains how the project embodies the maison's long-term commitment to sustainability, terroir and innovation. Rebecca Lo reports.

The post Why Billecart-Salmon waited 208 years to make a Ratafia appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
As Maison Billecart-Salmon gears up to launch its inaugural Ratafia Champenois in Asia this autumn, seventh generation owner Mathieu Roland-Billecart explains how the project embodies the maison's long-term commitment to sustainability, terroir and innovation. Rebecca Lo reports. At a spring Maison Billecart-Salmon Champagne pairing dinner held at Tébo in Hong Kong, the hottest topic around the table quickly became what was not on the menu.  Regional sales manager Thibault Casoli could barely contain his excitement that the maison will launch its Ratafia Champenois in Asia – a completely new product for the centuries-old family business. After making its global debut at Rosewood Amsterdam in the spring, Billecart-Salmon’s interpretation of Ratafia will grace key Asia-Pacific on-trade partner venues in autumn 2026. These include Rosewood Hong Kong, Agnes in Brisbane, and still to be confirmed leading hospitality establishments in Singapore and Shanghai. At 18% ABV, the Ratafia contains four Champagne vintages from 2019 through 2022, produced by mutage of Pinot Noir grape must with Fine de Champagne. It was aged in mature Burgundy oak casks before being evenly divided between 500mL and 5L Dame Jeanne bottles. The 500mL is priced in France at €58 (£49.50), with prices in Asia-Pacific still to be set.  The Dame Jeannes were designed for select hospitality venues including Domaine Les Crayères and Arbane in Reims, Alléno in Paris, The Connaught Hotel in London, and the Waterside Inn in Bray. The 500mL bottles will be distributed across independent retail outlets, top restaurants, and 5-star hotels in key Billecart-Salmon markets starting early in 2027. 

Maximising terroir, minimising waste

For seventh generation owner and Maison Billecart-Salmon head Mathieu Roland-Billecart, Ratafia aligned with Look Beyond, the company’s CSR vision of maximising terroir while minimising waste. As the maison only uses juice from its first press for all its Champagnes (dubbed its cuvées), the discussion about what to do with second and third presses came up at a round table committee discussion.  “We concluded that the best use of these presses was Ratafia, as it needs more richness in the juice to balance the alcohol needed for the mutage,” recalled Roland-Billecart.  Rather than rely on focus groups and consumer surveys, Billecart-Salmon’s decision to produce Ratafia was instinctive: it was about crafting another unique taste experience from its Champagne terroir.  “The inaugural production is only two barrels, so it is mainly offered to loyal partners,” explained Roland-Billecart. “We don’t expect to advertise outside our own social media platforms. This may be very different to market-driven producers and kind of old school, but it works for us.  “We started the experiment from the 2019 harvest – my second harvest in charge – with fruit from Clos Saint Hilaire where traditionally our best experiments began. The fully biodynamically farmed grape is 100% Pinot Noir, the king grape varietal in our village of Mareuil-sur-Aÿ.”

Production process

Pinot Noir must from a single vineyard parcel was blended with Fine de Champagne at 60% ABV, raising the alcohol content of the wine and naturally halting the fermentation of sugars in the must.  “When we carried out our first blending trials at the end of 2025, each vintage brought its own distinctive contribution: 2019 for its richness and depth; 2020 for its maturity; 2021 for its freshness; and 2022 for its length,” noted chief winemaker Florent Nys.  “The oldest component had benefited from six years of ageing, while the youngest had three years in oak. Together, these four vintages created the most harmonious and expressive blend, revealing the signature balance and elegance of our maison.”  Nys felt that the Ratafia is a faithful reflection of Billecart-Salmon’s origin. In the glass, it offers aromas of orange peel, dark chocolate, ripe yellow fruit, and delicate smoky sweetness notes – all expressions of the character and identity commonly associated with Clos Saint-Hilaire.  For Nys, being part of Ratafia’s creation has been inspiring: “My biggest reward was to witness the birth of the first Billecart-Salmon Ratafia and see that it really appealed to our customers.”  

Second edition of Ratafia in the works

Billecart-Salmon Ratafia exists in its own category separate from the maison’s traditional Brut Réserve, Brut Rosé, Brut Le Blanc de Blancs and Barrel-vinified cuvées. It was designed to be enjoyed after a meal, with food pairings or in a cocktail.  The love story and 1818 marriage between Nicolas François Billecart and Elisabeth Salmon continue to resonate in Mareuil-sur-Aÿ with Billecart-Salmon’s efforts towards responsible winemaking. As it prepares for the eighth generation of owners, its Ratafia is a step towards maintaining the estate at its peak.   “We are already working on the second edition of Ratafia, with bottling scheduled for the end of 2026,” revealed Nys. “Our ambition is to craft an exceptional Ratafia every year, while remaining true to the identity of Billecart-Salmon and allowing each edition to reflect its unique character.” “As with all our wines, we simply released our first Ratafia when we feel we have created a great wine that’s ready to be shared,” said Roland-Billecart. “We make the most of being a family owned and operated maison for more than 208 years. We have the luxury of time.”

title: Wales bids for world’s first natural wine appellation
summary:
Britain could become home to the world’s first appellation dedicated to natural wine, with Welsh producers seeking protected status for wines made without synthetic chemicals, additives or industrial yeasts. The proposed Natural Wine of Wales PGI would also require grapes to be grown and spontaneously fermented in Wales.

The post Wales bids for world’s first natural wine appellation appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Britain could become home to the world’s first appellation dedicated to natural wine, with Welsh producers seeking protected status for wines made without synthetic chemicals, additives or industrial yeasts. The proposed Natural Wine of Wales PGI would also require grapes to be grown and spontaneously fermented in Wales. Britain could soon become home to the world’s first natural wine appellation, with Welsh winemakers pushing for an innovative protected geographical indication scheme that would recognise and protect terroir-led Welsh wine. The proposed Natural Wine of Wales PGI rules would exclude the use of synthetic chemicals, processing aids, additives and industrial yeasts in wine production. Sulphur inputs would be limited in quantity and permitted only at bottling. Wines would be made in Wales from spontaneously fermented grapes grown in Wales under organic practices on certified organic, regenerative or biodynamic estates. Paul Rolt, winemaker and owner of Hebron Vineyard in Carmarthenshire, said Welsh natural winemakers wanted to set environmental standards as part of their battle against greenwashing and ultra-processed wine. “For consumers, enjoying a Natural Wine of Wales will mean they know they are drinking a raw, fermented grape product, providing an honest and healthy representation of each vineyard, a taste of that place, unadulterated by synthetic chemicals either in the vineyard or in the winery.”

Calls for ingredient labelling

“We would like to see wine ingredients listed via QR codes or directly on labels. It is important that consumers know the nature of their product. They have a right to know,” Rolt continued. “In Britain, producers can currently make wine using 60 products, but consumers are unaware of this. Current labelling rules mean there is no obligation to list ingredients or processing aids.” Unlike their EU counterparts, UK wine producers are not obliged to list wine ingredients. Rolt heads a producers’ group backing the Natural Wine of Wales PGI application. It includes Richard Morris and Jean de Plessis, the owner and winemaker respectively at Ancre Hill Estate in Monmouth, Wales’s largest vineyard, and David Morris, producer of Mountain People Wines.

Future-proofing Welsh viticulture

Rolt said the Natural Wine of Wales PGI would provide Welsh producers working in a changing climate with greater choice over where to register their vineyards and production. It would also give consumers greater transparency over how the grapes were grown and the wines made. “We are climatically on the margins of viticulture in Wales. The growing of grape varieties is particularly site-specific here due to our geographical location and average rainfall levels, so we would like to establish a Natural Wine of Wales PGI that includes PIWI grape varieties to help future-proof viticulture here in a changing climate,” Rolt said. “Getting consistent yields each harvest is difficult in Wales. We need varieties that work here.”

Defra considers application

Rolt said he had received “positive feedback” this year from the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, having submitted the PGI application in August 2025. It is understood that Defra’s Geographical Indication Scrutiny Panel of Experts has made several observations after assessing the application. A Defra spokesperson told the drinks business that the Natural Wine of Wales PGI remained subject to the applicants providing further information.

Inspired by France’s natural wine rules

Rolt said the Natural Wine of Wales PGI application had been partly inspired by the Raw Wine Charter and France’s Vin Méthode Nature label, both of which exclude machine harvesting. France introduced the Vin Méthode Nature label in 2020 and prohibited the words “vin nature” from appearing on wine labels. French VMN winemakers can use one of two logos on bottles: one stating VMN and another stating VMN with less than 30mg of added sulphur.

Challenging the existing Welsh wine rules

The existing Welsh wine PGI allows up to 15% of a wine to be made from grapes grown in England. Much Welsh wine is also produced at English wineries, including Halfpenny Green in Staffordshire and Three Choirs in Gloucestershire. Rolt, however, challenged the idea that such wines could be considered terroir-led. “How can a wine be terroir-led if it is not made in the country? Rules that allow Welsh wine to be made in England have stifled winery investment in Wales,” he said.

title: How service crop management could save vineyards in dry years
summary:
A recent study on organic vineyards in Occitanie, France, showed how managing service crops can balance their soil-anchoring qualities against vine performance. Among four options studied, one stood out for preventing water stress in the vines.

The post How service crop management could save vineyards in dry years appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content: A recent study on organic vineyards in Occitanie, France, showed how managing service crops can balance their soil-anchoring qualities against vine performance. Among four options studied, one stood out for preventing water stress in the vines. Adding to the literature around sustainable viticulture and climate change adaptation, a study published in journal OENO One has examined the effect of service crop management on vineyards. Comparing both methods of management and timing of intervention, it sought to identify the effects on vine health through metrics such as yield, vigour and water stress. In essence, the study examined the trade-off necessary in putting service crops (non-agricultural plants that benefit the vineyard) between rows of vines. Such service crops (also termed cover crops) are known to anchor the soil, preventing erosion, and lessening soil compaction from machinery. However, as an added species in a designated area, they can compete with vines for water. Over three years from 2022 to 2024, the study assessed the impact of four different means of managing service crops. These varied according to timing (around budburst or one month after budburst) and the method (a mower in combination with superficial tillage or a roller-crimper). There was also a control treatment, consisting of bare soil with tillage employed. A careful balance Although the study cannot be extrapolated to universal inferences, it offers an insight into management practices in Mediterranean climates. The network of seven fields was located in Occitanie, in southern France; they experienced typical Mediterranean conditions of warm dry summers and rainfall concentrated in the winter months. The vineyards were also managed organically – significant, as sustainable practices (particularly regenerative farming) often employ cover crops between rows. The study supplements anecdotal evidence that cover crops can help vines survive drought – a particular issue with increasingly dramatic heatwaves in southern Europe. The standout management technique proved to be early intervention using the mower and tillage. This maintained the benefits of the cover crops over wetter winter weather, but caused no water stress or production loss compared to the control treatment. The late interventions and those using the roller-crimper all reduced yields, berry weight and vigour. The authors, in their conclusions, were keen to stress that the results were context-dependent. The participatory programme, using working farms, meant that a number of variables – for instance, soil type or microclimate – could not be separated from the results. Yet they did identify statistically significant impacts of these management techniques. Moreover, despite the risks of protocol deviation and data gaps, they found the collaborative approach and collective discussion – inherent to researching with working farms – to have positively impacted the research. Just as important as the scientific data was the proof that such studies have their place in safeguarding vineyards against climate change.

title: Wildfires threaten wineries as blaze nears Bordeaux
summary:
Wildfires have advanced towards the outskirts of Bordeaux as France battles blazes that have already forced hundreds of thousands of people to evacuate, with experts fearing this year’s vintage could be damaged by smoke taint. 

The post Wildfires threaten wineries as blaze nears Bordeaux appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Wildfires have advanced towards the outskirts of Bordeaux as France battles blazes that have already forced hundreds of thousands of people to evacuate, with experts fearing this year’s vintage could be damaged by smoke taint.  More than 220,000 people have been evacuated in France, where fires have swept across the Cap Ferret peninsula on the Atlantic coast, a popular tourist destination, and spread through areas surrounding the city of Bordeaux. Bordeaux Mayor Thomas Cazenave said the blaze was "at the gates of the metropolitan area", coming within around 15 kilometres of the city. The Gironde prefect ordered the partial closure of a major motorway serving Bordeaux. This morning, President Macron is holding a crisis meeting to discuss next steps regarding the blazes across southern France.  Despite the proximity of the fire, Cazenave said there were no plans to evacuate the city, which has a population of around 268,000.

Smoke taint concerns

Thousands of firefighters, supported by specialised water-bombing aircraft, have been deployed to tackle the fast-moving fires and thick smoke. However, shifting winds and hot, dry conditions have hampered efforts to contain the blazes, which have burned out of control since midweek in the Gironde region. The threat posed to Bordeaux’s vineyards is, so far, unclear. According to experts, smoke taint poses a major concern. This is when smoke particles cling to grape skins, resulting in an unwanted flavour that is believed to harm wine quality, particularly in red varieties. On Saturday night, around 55,000 people were evacuated from villages south of Gironde, an area internationally regarded for its wine production. Across Europe, wildfires have continued to burn amid prolonged heat and drought. France and Spain have together evacuated more than 330,000 people over the past week as emergency services battle multiple fires. French authorities also confirmed that a man had been arrested on suspicion of breaking into an evacuated home and stealing 44 bottles of fine wine while residents had fled the fires.

Uncertain future

Interior minister Laurent Nunez told France 2 television that the situation remained critical. "We have a fire that is not under control and which is moving in the direction of the city area," he said. "The overall situation is very unfavourable. We are in a situation that is unprecedented." Gironde prefect Sophie Brocas has called for visitors to avoid the region until conditions improve. "We urge tourists not to come to this region, at least until the situation is under control," she said. Sebastien Berge, head of the Gironde fire service, said the scale of the blaze made it particularly difficult to predict. "When there's a fire of this magnitude, it creates its own weather pattern. It's difficult to monitor," he said.

National emergency declared in Spain

Meanwhile, in Spain, where a national emergency has been declared, firefighters reported some progress as more favourable weather conditions helped slow merging wildfires outside Madrid. Scientists say climate change is increasing the likelihood and intensity of extreme weather events such as heatwaves and wildfires.  Coming at the height of the summer holiday season, the fires have been fuelled by forests left tinder-dry after successive heatwaves and months of below-average rainfall.

title: Wildfires threaten historic vineyards in Sierra de Gredos
summary:
More than 50,000 hectares have burned in Ávila as producers wait to discover the extent of the damage to Sierra de Gredos’ old-vine Garnacha and Albillo Real vineyards. Several historic parcels have already been lost as firefighters continue to battle one of Spain’s most destructive recent wildfires.

The post Wildfires threaten historic vineyards in Sierra de Gredos appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
More than 50,000 hectares have burned in Ávila as producers wait to discover the extent of the damage to Sierra de Gredos’ old-vine Garnacha and Albillo Real vineyards. Several historic parcels have already been lost as firefighters continue to battle one of Spain’s most destructive recent wildfires. Residents, winegrowers and firefighters across Sierra de Gredos – which is around 150km west of Madrid – are battling one of the most destructive wildfires in Spain’s recent history. As of Sunday, 26 July, the Burgohondo fire remained active, although its main perimeter had been contained, with several fronts still burning. The latest estimates suggest that it has affected more than 50,000 hectares in the province of Ávila and forced thousands of residents to evacuate their homes or remain confined. The region, internationally renowned for its old-vine Garnacha and Albillo Real, remains under severe pressure. Firefighters have been working to control the blaze since it began near Burgohondo last Wednesday. It is still too early to assess the full extent of the damage to vineyards. Many producers remain unable to enter the affected areas, while others are only now beginning to discover what has been lost.

Historic San Gregorio vineyard damaged

Among the vineyard losses confirmed so far is the San Gregorio vineyard belonging to Bodega El Reventón, owned by Adrianna Catena, Alejandro Vigil and Gearóid Lane. The old-vine parcel, which produces one of the estate’s top wines, has suffered extensive fire damage. “We have suffered huge damage to our historic San Gregorio vineyard, whose wonderful grapes make one of our two single-parcel wines,” said Gearóid Lane, co-founder of Bodega El Reventón. “We are working to assess the extent of the damage to these old vines, some of which date back to the 1920s. We are heartbroken, but Alejandro, Adrianna and I are unwavering in our dedication to this wonderful region.”

Cebreros vineyards exposed

Cebreros is among the wine-growing areas exposed to the fire. Chuchi Soto, founder of Soto Manrique and manager of the local cooperative winery, has also lost one of his vineyards to the flames and is awaiting news of his other plots. “The vineyards in the Gredos area lie in mountainous terrain surrounded by woodland,” Soto told the drinks business. “They are small plots enclosed by trees and vegetation that are left to grow unchecked. This is what makes the area so distinctive, but also so dangerous.” “In Spain, the laws protecting woodland are very strict, and the vegetation is allowed to grow freely. If we take action ourselves, we are fined. As things stand, it is difficult even to gain access when trying to put out a fire.”

Firebreaks protect Indiano Wines parcel

Indiano Wines lost several old vines when the fire encircled one of its vineyards over the weekend. Thanks to the team’s work clearing undergrowth and keeping the vineyard floor clean, however, the flames did not advance further into the plot, instead burning the surrounding forest. “The problem is the lack of resources to manage the land and care for the region throughout the year,” said Indiano co-founder and viticulturist Charly Gotchac. “We need the firebreaks to be maintained throughout the year. They are vital. We keep our vineyards clear so that we can harvest fruit, but the same needs to be true of all cultivated and forested land: the pine plantations, chestnut groves and olive groves. Today, that is not the case.” “We are in a poor region with few resources, and one that is being abandoned by the younger generation,” Gotchac added. “This creates risks for the future. And it is only 26 July. We still have all of August ahead of us, which is the highest-risk month.”

Irreplaceable viticultural heritage at risk

The damage to Gredos’ irreplaceable viticultural heritage will not be measurable until the fire has been extinguished and producers can return safely to their vineyards. For those on the ground, however, there is little doubt that the landscape has already been profoundly changed. “The Gredos we know and love no longer exists,” said Bárbara Requejo, winemaker and co-founder of Las Pedreras. “This catastrophe, which seems to have no end, has destroyed our landscape, our greatest asset, and will have catastrophic consequences for the region’s economy. I hope that we, winegrowers, winemakers, livestock farmers and those working in hospitality, will be able to act together and demand from the authorities the support we need.”

Region remains in shock

The region remains in shock, with residents and producers waiting anxiously for the fires to be brought under control. “We are still in shock, and there is no system in place yet to raise funds,” Gotchac added. “The damage is so enormous that we do not even know who to help first. Many people have lost everything: their businesses, homes, farms and animals.” “We are waiting for the wind to drop and the fires to abate, but that has not happened yet. We are still in the middle of the emergency.” At the time of publication, no dedicated fundraising initiative had been established for the Gredos wine community. In the meantime, buying wines from the region and supporting its producers offers one immediate way for the wine trade and consumers to show solidarity. Amanda Barnes MW is the drinks business’ regular South America correspondent and author of The South America Wine Guide.

title: AB InBev’s Grupo Modelo builds US$760 million Mexican brewery
summary:
Grupo Modelo, owned by AB InBev, is building a brewing and bottling complex in Mexico’s city of Apan, in the state of Hidalgo, investing around MXN14 billion (US$760 million).

The post AB InBev’s Grupo Modelo builds US$760 million Mexican brewery appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Grupo Modelo, owned by AB InBev, is building a brewing and bottling complex in Mexico’s city of Apan, in the state of Hidalgo, investing around MXN14 billion (US$760 million). The site, which is set to give the beer giant integrated and boosted capacity in central Mexico, has been designed to meet an initial capacity of up to 12 million hectolitres a year, which will make it among Grupo Modelo’s largest facilities globally.

Meeting demand

Mexican beer brands like Corona have experienced massive popularity and market shifts in the US of late, largely driven by hipster lifestyle branding and shifting sales dominance connected to import and tariff pressures. According to reports from the Rio Times, the scale supports both domestic demand for beer, but is also set to boost Mexico’s beer exports with the market already being the world’s top beer exporter with Corona as its flagship brand. Assisting the Mexican market, the move has meant that the construction of the brewery site has offered work to more than 4,500 workers to assist in the build. In addition to this, more than 600 people in Mexico have also already been hired and trained to run the beer and bottling plant.

Part of the wider plan

According to AB InBev, the Hidalgo plant is one piece of its Grupo Modelo pledge to invest more than US$3.6 billion in Mexico between 2025 and 2027. Despite these forward moves, one of the US largest unions, The International Brotherhood of Teamsters, has recently reiterated that it wants Trump to impose tariffs on Mexican beer and has reportedly stated that more of it should be brewed by US workers instead of being made across the border. db has reached out to AB InBev for further insight into the investment and the export plans for the site.

title: Rathfinny wins approval to expand Sussex wine tourism offering
summary:
Rathfinny Wine Estate has secured planning approval to expand its accommodation offering, adding new luxury stays and refurbishing existing facilities as demand for English wine tourism continues to grow.

The post Rathfinny wins approval to expand Sussex wine tourism offering appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Rathfinny Wine Estate has secured planning approval to expand its accommodation offering, adding new luxury stays and refurbishing existing facilities as demand for English wine tourism continues to grow.

Rathfinny Wine Estate has received unanimous planning approval from the South Downs National Park Authority to expand its guest accommodation as it looks to meet growing demand for wine tourism in Sussex.

The English sparkling wine producer, which is set within a 600-acre vineyard in the South Downs, said the development forms the next stage of its ambition to establish the region as a leading wine tourism destination for both UK and international visitors.

The estate has welcomed overnight guests for more than a decade, offering vineyard accommodation alongside winery tours, tastings, dining experiences and its Cellar Door shop. The latest expansion will increase capacity and introduce new accommodation options overlooking the vineyards.

New accommodation and refurbishment plans

Under the approved plans, Rathfinny will add six luxury 'Grape Pickers' Huts' in the estate's former quarry, overlooking the vineyard. A new Stable Block will also be built, providing four guest bedrooms with private terraces offering views across the South Downs.

The estate will also refurbish its existing Flint Barns accommodation, enlarging guest rooms to create more spacious accommodation. A new dining room and vineyard-facing terrace will also be added.

During the planning process, councillors praised both the quality of the architectural designs and Rathfinny's sustainable approach to development. The producer, which achieved B Corp certification in 2023, said the investment reflects its long-term commitment to responsible growth.

The expansion comes as Sussex continues to strengthen its reputation as a cool-climate wine region, with the Sussex Winelands attracting increasing numbers of visitors, particularly from Scandinavia and North America. Rathfinny noted that accommodation within the South Downs National Park remains limited despite growing international interest in the region.

Investment to create hospitality jobs

Alongside increasing visitor capacity, the project is expected to create new jobs within Rathfinny's hospitality business. Recruitment has already begun for several positions, including a Flint Barns Manager and additional Food & Beverage supervisors.

Mark Driver, co-owner and co-founder of Rathfinny, said: "When we planted our first vines, we always dreamed of creating far more than a vineyard. We wanted Rathfinny to be a place where people could stay, dine, tour and discover the remarkable quality of Sussex Sparkling wine."

He added: "This investment allows us to welcome more guests than ever before to the estate and to share everything that makes Sussex such a special place to visit. We're incredibly grateful for the support of the South Downs National Park Authority and excited to bring these exceptional new accommodation spaces to life."

Driver continued: "English wine tourism is entering a new era. Visitors from around the world are discovering Sussex as one of the most exciting wine destinations anywhere, and we're proud to be helping shape that future while creating new opportunities for hospitality careers in the region."

title: Why gin is being served with afternoon tea
summary:
Gin being served with afternoon tea has become an upscale alcoholic twist on the ritual. db finds out more about the trend.

The post Why gin is being served with afternoon tea appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Gin being served with afternoon tea has become an upscale alcoholic twist on the ritual. db finds out more about the trend. Both gin and tea have long histories as traditional hosting centrepieces for gatherings. They also share botanical roots and a history as social lubricants, but will we see more of the pairing? According to the Gin Guild, the partnership is here to stay.

Occasion, botanicals, presentation

Speaking to the drinks business, The Gin Guild director general Pal Gleed said: “The pairing of gin and afternoon tea feels entirely natural because both are deeply rooted in British food and drink culture. Afternoon tea celebrates a sense of occasion, delicate flavours, fragrant botanicals and careful presentation - qualities that are equally at the heart of a well-made gin.” Gleed explained to db that “many classic gin botanicals, such as juniper, citrus peel, coriander seed and floral ingredients, complement the aromas found in fine teas, preserves and traditional pastries. Whether enjoyed as a classic gin and tonic or in a cocktail, gin can enhance rather than overpower the experience”.

Elegance

The ritual of serving gins alongside teas could also be continuing to thrive right now because “there's also an element of theatre,” said Gleed and pointed out that “afternoon tea has always been about taking time to enjoy good company in elegant surroundings, and gin has long been associated with hospitality and celebration”. Describing why the union of gin and afternoon tea shows promise, Eden Mill Distillery, based in Scotland, reiterated how the two offer a lot of versatility and complementary flavours. Eden Mill CEO Steven Kersley told db: “Gin remains one of the most versatile spirits when it comes to food pairing, and afternoon tea is a perfect example. The freshness of citrus and botanicals cuts through rich pastries while complementing fruit and floral flavours, making it an ideal match for a modern afternoon tea.”

Afternoon Tea Week

Eden Mill recently launched Summer in St Andrews, a limited edition coastal Scottish gin inspired by the flavours of the distillery’s hometown during the sunny months. Bottled at 40% ABV, the gin is designed for long afternoons by the sea: poured long with tonic and a lemon wheel, or spritzed up with soda, fizz and lemon. Explaining more, Eden Mill senior brand manager Hamish Maclean said: "Local raspberries and strawberries from Tarvit Farm in Cupar are bolstered by heady rhubarb and a sharp kick of lemon.” The launch will be celebrated at the distillery during Afternoon Tea Week (10-16 August) with a Summer Gin Afternoon Tea service on offer throughout the month of August. Additionally, cakes and preserves will be paired with the gin which will be available as a Bramble serve and will be poured tableside from a teapot. Each of the tickets will be priced at £35 per person and will be available via the distillery website. Similarly, the Warwickshire Gin Company, based in Leamington Spa, also offers an "Afternoon G&T" experience featuring a welcome G&T, traditional afternoon tea, and a local distillery tour. Also, Denbies Wine Estate in Surrey hosts seasonal "Gin in the Vines" events combining a local gin tasting with a sparkling afternoon tea overlooking the vineyard. Plus, venues such as those owned by multiple operator Future Inns, which has sites based in Cardiff and Plymouth, feature discounted G&T or cocktail afternoon tea options priced from £25.50 per person during August too.

Quintessentially British

According to a spokesperson from Pernod Ricard-owned Beefeater Gin, the pairing works well because tea and gin both “share botanical roots, and their flavour profiles naturally complement each other”. This is because “both beverages feature herbal, floral, and piney elements that blend smoothly without clashing”. “Bergamot in Earl Grey tea brings out the bright citrus peel notes found in many gins” and “the pine-like punch of juniper in gin cuts through the rich, buttery textures of clotted cream and pastries” while “chamomile or floral tea blends match the delicate, sweet side of lighter craft gins,” said the spokesperson. Gleed also told db that the trend will continue because “it's a pairing that feels quintessentially British while continuing to evolve in modern hotels, bars and restaurants” a move that is both retaining its historical roots, while also amplifying it as a serve that still offers a sense of celebration now and for the future.
